title: The ‘glass skin’ Korean beauty trend has risks, experts warn
content: Greta Costioli was once known as the “ glass skin girl ” on TikTok. Following the Korean beauty trend, Costioli would layer on product after product — toners, serums, essences and moisturizers — in pursuit of an ultra-dewy complexion. Costioli, age 29, said that ever since she was a teenager she would apply extra moisturizer for her naturally dry complexion. When the “glass skin” trend became popular on social media, she fully leaned in, including trying one method requiring seven different layers of hydrating toner. It may sound excessive, but that kind of elaborate skin care routine has become increasingly popular across TikTok and Instagram, where beauty influencers routinely film themselves using skincare products to achieve the glossy, almost reflective complexion known as “glass skin.” Celebrities including Kylie Jenner and Hailey Bieber have amplified the trend, posting their regimens that resulted in similar dewy skin. The glass skin trend has its roots in South Korean beauty culture, where the term is used to describe a complexion that appears exceptionally smooth and pore-less. The phrase appears to have first come around in the early to mid-2010s and then saw a major spike at the end of 2025 going into 2026, according to Google trends . Those who subscribe to the complex routines say their skin benefits from the layers of hydration, and viewers are hooked on the ASMR-like videos as influencers tap their glass-like faces with their fingers and beauty tools. Certain aspects of the glass skin routine, such as moisturizing and using sunscreen, are positive steps toward safe skincare, according to the American Academy of Dermatology. However, problems occur when people use too many products, which can lead to issues such as clogged pores, irritation and breakouts, the association said. Because of the trend’s rising popularity, dermatologists are warning others that the glass skin look may be unrealistic and the skincare routines behind it aren’t suitable for every skin type. Experts also point out that many of the videos contain advice from non-medical influencers, leading to a lack of basic safety information. New research presented September 29 at the European Academy of Dermatology and Venereology (EADV) Congress 2026 found that nearly 95% of the most viral videos on the trend contained misleading claims. “We expected to find some gaps in the quality of the information, but I was surprised by how consistent they were,” Dr. Maria Lúcia Paysano, co-lead author of the study and a dermatology resident at the Professor Rubem David Azulay Institute of Dermatology in Brazil, said in an email. The study authors screened the top videos across five Korean skincare-related search terms. After exclusions, 38 videos were assessed for dermatological claims and safety information using the Global Quality Scale and modified DISCERN, a tool used to assess the quality and reliability of health information. Out of the 38 videos analyzed, only one video mentioned irritation risk, two addressed sun protection and none mentioned contact dermatitis risk or advised consulting a dermatologist, according to the study. About 45% recommended combining several active ingredients without safety advice, and 32% promised immediate results. Overall, none of the videos were produced by dermatologists, according to the study. “Problems can arise when complex, one-size-fits-all routines encourage the use of multiple active ingredients without considering individual skin type, tolerance or irritation risk. A skincare routine should prioritize skin health and barrier function rather than simply trying to reproduce a viral appearance,” Paysano said. The bottom line is you can take it too far. For Costioli, who posts her skincare journey on social media, her glass skin routine initially worked well for her, but soon she started having adverse reactions. “At first my skin really loved it, because I have dry skin and my skin absorbs skincare really well. I got a lot of compliments from people online and offline on how great my skin looked,” Costioli said in an email. “However, I kept compromising my skin barrier quite often, because I was simply using too many products.” For her, a broken skin barrier looked like small red bumps on her face that would last for a few days. But if she continued with the extensive routines, the bumps would get more aggressive. “It wasn’t something I could keep up doing, so I had to reduce the steps in my skincare routine,” she said. Experts agree that Korean skincare is not the problem. The concern is that social media can turn simple skincare practices into trendy and complex routines that may not work safely for everyone. “The proof is in the pudding: none of these videos were created by dermatologists, so it should not be a shock that omissions and misinformation are ensued,” Dr. Mona Gohara, a board-certified dermatologist and clinical professor in the department of dermatology at Yale School of Medicine, said in an email. Gohara, who was not involved with the new study, added that many skincare trends, not just the glass skin, have amplified voices that are not medically trained. Additionally, achieving pore-less skin is not possible, as pores are genetic and do not respond to layering products, said Dr. Jane Yoo, a board-certified dermatologist and Mohs surgeon based in New York City. “When patients try to attain this goal, they may inadvertently be disrupting their skin cycle as the physiologic exfoliation signals are now removed,” said Yoo, who is an assistant clinical professor at the Icahn School of Medicine at Mount Sinai. Yoo was also not involved with the study. Common skin issues she observes with her patients who have utilized too many products include contact dermatitis, rosacea and acne flares. Tight, itchy, tender, inflamed, flakey or scaly, and red or darker skin are all signs that someone’s skin barrier may be damaged, added Gohara. To help your skin recover, she recommends pausing scrubs, exfoliating acids and retinoids, and instead cleansing with a gentle, pH neutral, non-soap cleanser and lukewarm water. She added that barrier repair creams can help, and to keep applying sunscreen during the day. “It’s great to have patients educated on their skin but it’s not a one-size-fits-all approach. You have to know your skin type and work with a dermatologist to see if these products are right for you,” added Yoo. The good news is, “you can pursue the glow while taking care of the skin beneath it,” Gohara said. She recommends moisturizing often, especially as skin can become drier with age and hormone changes. To boost that dewy look, layer from lightest to heaviest with a light, concentrated hydrating hyaluronic acid serum, followed by a moisturizer and then a barrier repair cream. Yoo, who is a Korean American dermatologist, often tells patients that they do not need a complex routine for their skin. She typically recommends a four-step approach, including a simple cleanser, an active – such as retinol, Salicylic acid or Vitamin C – a moisturizer and SPF. “The key is to know thy skin and know what it can tolerate,” Gohara said. “Add one product at a time, start slowly, and wear broad-spectrum SPF 30 or higher every day. Sun damage is one of the biggest vibrance killers, along with stress, smog, smoking, lack of sleep, and yes sugar.”
ranking_reason: The 'glass skin' trend may lead to skin problems and misinformation, highlighting the importance of seeking professional advice and prioritizing skin health.

analysis.reason: The 'glass skin' trend may lead to skin problems and misinformation, highlighting the importance of seeking professional advice and prioritizing skin health.

title: The radical idea that temperature sets when we sleep
content:
Some scientists think that temperature could be just as important as light at training the body's circadian clocks.
Even today, anthropologist Gandhi Yetish remembers the bedtime ritual he had as a child during cold New Jersey winters. He would open his window, letting the frigid air rush in and cool his face. He'd quickly feel drowsier, though he'd wonder what his mother would say about the heating bill.
There's emerging evidence that Yetish was onto something. From how deeply we sleep to how refreshed we feel afterwards, temperature can have a profound impact on our nightly rest. Some scientists are even going one step further, arguing that temperature may be as important as light for shaping when we sleep.
Here's what we do and don't know.
For years, Yetish thought his preference for cool sleeping quarters was a personal quirk. Then, while researching the sleep of people in non-industrial societies, he spent time with the Tsimane, an indigenous group in Bolivia's Amazon.
Yetish was keenly aware of the long-held scientific consensus that the most important environmental cue for sleep was light exposure. But he found that the Tsimane typically went to sleep hours after sunset and rose before sunrise, despite lacking electricity for artificial lighting and spending most of their days outdoors.
Next, Yetish and a team of colleagues from universities across the US investigated the sleep of two other indigenous groups. These included the Hadza of northern Tanzania and the San in Southern Africa. The researchers found that their sleep timings also didn't correspond with light and dark cycles. Instead, it seemed to be tracking the rise and fall of the ambient temperature.
"We assume that the reason the sunset and sunrise are important is because of the light," says Yetish. "Well, temperature also comes from the Sun."
Decades of evidence shows that our core body temperature begins to drop as we wind down for sleep. For most of us, it continues to decline for much of the night, usually falling by around 1C from its daytime high to nighttime low.
How to Sleep Better
Want to wake up rested and feel more alert? Sign up to How to Sleep Better , our free six-part email course which features expert tips on how to improve your sleep.
This helps explain why people often experience shortened, more disturbed sleep when their room isn't cool enough, says Sebastian Herberger, a sleep physician and scientist at the Interdisciplinary Center of Sleep Medicine in Berlin. "Everyone who's ever slept in a hotel room that's too hot would potentially know these kinds of effects," he says.
For a 2007 study , researchers changed the temperature of the room participants slept in to investigate its effects. The group experienced two different sleep set-ups. In one experiment, they were provided with a room where the temperature lowered from 27C (81F) to 24C (75F) from 18:00 to 22:00, slowly rose to 27C between 03:00 and 07:00, and then remained at 27C during the day. This was to mimic the natural rise and fall of the ambient temperature through the night. In the other experiment, they slept in a room at a constant 27C.
When they slept in fluctuating temperatures, the participants had higher levels of a marker of melatonin overnight, compared to those who slept at a steady 27C. This hormone is produced by the body naturally, increasing in the lead-up to sleep time and usually reaching its peak in the middle of the night. It tells your body to wind down and prepare for sleep.
The same group also felt more refreshed when they awoke. The researchers speculated that we evolved to have deeper sleep under the influence of the natural temperature fluctuations at dusk and dawn.
However, the ideal temperature drop required to drift off to sleep is not yet clear – and how much temperature might impact our body clocks and sleep timings is still being debated.
One question raised by the potential link between temperature and sleep is whether, and how much, it can help to set our internal body clocks. These clocks coordinate our  "circadian rhythms", cycles of mental, physical and behavioural changes that occur in any 24-hour period. This includes everything from when we sleep to when we eat. Circadian rhythms are traditionally thought to be dictated mainly by our exposure to light.
The circadian rhythm is the primary driver behind the fall in our body temperature in the lead-up to sleep, says Russell Foster, professor of circadian neuroscience at the University of Oxford and author of the book Life Time.
But Foster explains that temperature may not just be influenced by our body clocks – it may be an extra input that helps shape them, too. "What it's actually doing in terms of as a signal to the sleep systems, we don't know," he says.
Animal experiments have provided some evidence for the idea that temperature may itself be helping to set our body clocks.
ranking_reason: This discovery highlights the importance of temperature in shaping our sleep patterns and internal body clocks, which can have significant implications for public health and wellbeing.

analysis.reason: This discovery highlights the importance of temperature in shaping our sleep patterns and internal body clocks, which can have significant implications for public health and wellbeing.

title: Pneumonic plague, by the numbers
content: The World Health Organization said Wednesday that it had few clear answers about the recent death of a worker at a Russian institute that researched plague. The death, the subsequent isolation of hundreds of co-workers and close contacts, and reports that another worker may have pneumonia have fueled global concern about a rare form of plague. Here’s what we know about pneumonic plague by the numbers. One person who worked at the Irkutsk Research Anti-Plague Institute of Siberia in southeast Russia has died. There have also been media reports that a second employee of the lab has pneumonia of “undetermined cause,” the director-general of the World Health Organization said Wednesday. The 28-year-old who died was identified by the independent regional news outlet Lyudi Baikala as Darya Shipilova. Shipilova first went to the hospital September 29 in Shelekhov, a town 12 miles southwest of Irkutsk, where she worked. Three days later, on October 2 , she died. Rospotrebnadzor, the Russian agency that handles infectious disease, says the worker died of pneumonia of “unknown” origin and downplayed suspicions that her death was related to her work. WHO said it has seen about local media reports about an incident in the lab involving a broken test tube. Currently, “I know what you know from the media of the test tube breaking and exposure,” Dr. Maria Van Kerkhove, director of WHO’s department of Epidemic and Pandemic Management, said Wednesday. On October 2 , the Russian government held a meeting “because they suspected a resident of the Irkutsk Institute had contracted a dangerous infection,” WHO Director-General Dr. Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus said Wednesday. WHO said it first heard about the patient because it uses AI to monitor local news reports for illnesses of concern. Under international law, Russia should have reported the incident within 24 hours . After the WHO sought more information about the death, the Russian Federation replied Tuesday to say that that “ no case of plague had recently been reported.” The Russian government also said it placed about 200 people who’d had contact with the worker in quarantine or under close follow-up , WHO said. WHO said it had requested further information from the government, but has not received it. “We don’t have the full picture of this event, and we are not able to conduct a full risk assessment,” Tedros said. “Timely, complete and transparent information sharing under the international regulations is essential to clarify conflicting reports and enable an accurate assessment of potential public health risks.” A number of hospitals in the area have restricted visitors and are conducting comprehensive health checks, including requiring people to fill out questionnaires about “plague” and other infectious disease symptoms. Rospotrebnadzor, however, reassured people in the region where the lab operates that the “epidemiological situation” is stable. About 95 people work at the Anti-Plague Institute. The institute opened in 1934 to research plague. The bacterium that causes plague, Yersinia pestis, still circulates among wildlife in Siberia and neighboring regions. Globally, more than 200 kinds of mammals, mostly rodents, can contract Y. pestis, studies show . Marmots are the most common carriers in Siberia. WHO said the risk to the general public “appears to be low” at this time based on the limited information it has. There are thousands of suspected plague cases around the world every year, Van Kerkhove said. From 2019 to 2025, 10 countries reported almost 4,000 suspected human plague cases and 423 deaths , WHO said Wednesday. Central Asia has the largest number of foci, or areas where the disease is present. People are most often infected after exposure to infected rodents. There are four major types of plague caused by Y. pestis that attack different parts of the body: WHO said it conducted an initial assessment of risk based on an understanding that the Russian lab worker’s case could be pneumonic plague. Pneumonic plague is the only form of the bacterial infection that can spread from person to person. The basic reproduction number is about 1.1 to 1.3 , meaning that one person with pneumonic plague can spread the disease through a cough or sneeze to about 1.3 people , studies show . Droplets from infected animals can also transmit it. People can develop symptoms as soon as 24 hours after exposure, according to Dr. Rutul Dalal, an infectious disease physician at Penn State Health St. Joseph Medical Center. Typically, people with pneumonic plague are so sick that they rarely spread it because “it’s very difficult for someone to even walk, do their daily activities, let alone travel,” he said. There are no direct flights between Russia and the US, Dalal noted. By the time infected travelers reached the US, they would already be showing symptoms. “Of course, you have to be careful,” he said, because “the world is a little village now,” as everyone learned during the Covid-19 pandemic. Patients treated within the first 24 hours of infection have the best chance of surviving. People with plague typically get at least 10 to 14 days of antibiotics. Five antibiotics typically work best against plague: ciprofloxacin, levofloxacin, moxifloxacin, gentamicin and streptomycin. Doctors have used plague vaccines since the 19th century , but it’s not clear how protective they are against pneumonic plague. WHO doesn’t recommend vaccination except for high-risk groups and lab workers who are regularly exposed to the bacteria. The bacterium that causes plague circulates on every continent except Oceania. It has infected human populations for at least 5,000 years , studies of archaeological sites show. Three of the world’s deadliest pandemics were caused by Y. pestis. 1924 was the year of the last documented person-to-person transmission of pneumonic plague in the US, during an outbreak in Los Angeles. Since the 1990s, most human cases have been in Africa, according to WHO . July 2025 was when the last person in the US died from pneumonic plague. The person lived in Arizona and was probably infected while working with sick cats. In the US about five human cases are reported every year.
ranking_reason: The public should be aware of this event because it highlights the risk of pneumonic plague spreading and the importance of timely reporting and transparency in public health crises.

analysis.reason: The public should be aware of this event because it highlights the risk of pneumonic plague spreading and the importance of timely reporting and transparency in public health crises.
